claims.statement: create_deep_agent assembles an ordered list of AgentMiddleware and passes it to LangChain's create_agent(), which builds the actual model/tool loop; the harness adds a new runtime, only middleware.

Middleware overrides hooks such as wrap_model_call() that intercept every LLM request before it is sent, letting it filter tools, inject prompt context, transform history, and maintain typed cross-turn state.

A callable passed via tools= is only invoked after the model chooses to call it and cannot rewrite the tool list or prompt before the model call, whereas middleware runs before every model call; caller tools= are additive and never remove a built-in.

The main-agent stack is composed in three bands: base scaffolding is appended first, caller middleware from the middleware= param is spliced in the middle, and profile/tail middleware is appended last.

Tail middleware is ordered late because it reacts to the near-final request: harness-profile extras precede prompt caching, and MemoryMiddleware is placed after prompt caching so its system-prompt mutations do not invalidate the Anthropic cache prefix.

Prompt-caching middleware is appended unconditionally (Anthropic always, plus Bedrock/Fireworks when their integration packages are importable) and no-ops for models it does not apply to, so it can be installed but never fire for a given model.
Tool exclusion (_ToolExclusionMiddleware) is appended last so excluded tool names are stripped after all tool-injecting middleware and any caller wrap_model_call has run and cannot be restored.

Caller middleware is merged by name: an entry whose .name matches a base member replaces it in place preserving position, otherwise a new entry is inserted after the last core member so it precedes the profile/prompt-caching/memory tail.

FilesystemMiddleware and SubAgentMiddleware are registered as required scaffolding because they back the built-in file tools/permissions and the task tool handler; excluding them raises rather than producing a silently degraded agent.
A HarnessProfile can subtract members from the assembled stack via excluded_middleware, validated first to reject required scaffolding, then applied as a filter, then verified for coverage.

In exclusion filtering, class entries match on exact type (not isinstance) so a caller subclass survives when the base class is excluded, while string entries match AgentMiddleware.name exactly so a public alias can drop an impl class whose .name differs from __name__.
A string exclusion that matches more than one distinct class within a single stack raises ValueError, forcing disambiguation with a class-form exclusion.

A profile exclusion entry only needs to match somewhere across the stacks the profile applies to; matches are accumulated into shared sets across the main agent and general-purpose subagent stacks, and coverage is verified once after every stack has been filtered, raising if any entry matched nothing.

Each declarative SubAgent resolves its own model harness profile and independently assembles its middleware stack: filesystem, summarization, patch-tool calls, isolated-mode skills or forked parent skills, profile extras, prompt caching, two exclusion passes around spec middleware, coverage validation, and final tool exclusion; a fork additionally mirrors top-level memory when configured.
The auto-added general-purpose subagent is assembled with its own stack and inherits only caller middleware that overrides one of its default slots, not main-agent-specific middleware.

Subagents are routed by form at assembly time: entries with graph_id become AsyncSubAgents handled by AsyncSubAgentMiddleware, entries with runnable are CompiledSubAgents, and others are declarative SubAgents; delegated-only behavior therefore depends on which subagent type handled the task.

The main stack applies excluded_middleware before and after merging caller middleware, so a profile exclusion also removes a caller attempt to reintroduce an excluded class or name; excluded_tools is appended only after those passes.

Declarative subagents inherit top-level tools, permissions, and interrupt_on only when their specs omit the corresponding field; their own permissions replace rather than extend parent rules, and compilation appends HumanInTheLoopMiddleware when the resolved interrupt configuration is non-empty.

Compiled subagent runnables are used as supplied and do not inherit the parent state schema, while async subagents run remotely as background tasks that return a task ID and track task state through AsyncSubAgentMiddleware.
The main stack collects explicit and middleware-contributed state schemas, derives private state fields, and assigns them to SubAgentMiddleware for subagent dispatch.
SubAgent uses isolated context by default; handoff is accepted only as a legacy alias for isolated behavior, while fork is the experimental mode that continues the parent's conversation.

Fork invocation supplies the parent's effective history plus a task preamble; declarative forks retain non-excluded parent state including private channels, compiled forks strip private state, and forked children are refused if they recursively invoke task.

Tool exclusion removes named tools from model requests and rejects attempts to call those names at the tool-call boundary; the implementation explicitly describes this as execution consistency rather than a security surface.
Filesystem permissions are enforced by FilesystemMiddleware at built-in filesystem tool calls, not at the backend layer, so direct backend use does not incorporate these permission rules.

A compiled subagent result must contain messages; the parent returns a ToolMessage with a JSON-serialized structured response when present or the last non-empty AI text otherwise, and merges eligible non-private state updates.

Deep Agents summarization truncates large older tool arguments, compacts history when needed or after ContextOverflowError, offloads evicted history to the backend, and records the summary event and session ID in private state; an offload failure warns that older messages are unrecoverable.
